Pregnancy

Posterior cervix: position, labour and examinations

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing that your cervix is posterior can sound worrying, especially near your due date. It usually describes where the cervix lies during an examination, rather than a disease. Position is one piece of information: it cannot tell you exactly when labour will begin or whether your pregnancy is healthy.

What posterior and anterior mean

The cervix is the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. Posterior means directed towards the back of the pelvis; anterior means towards the front. Posterior does not mean towards the abdomen. A clinician may describe the cervix as posterior, central or anterior, alongside how open, long and firm it feels.

Cervical direction and the tilt of the whole uterus are related anatomical observations but are not interchangeable diagnoses. An anteverted uterus tilts forwards; a retroverted uterus tilts backwards. The word posterior applied to the cervix also does not describe the baby's head position, a posterior placenta, a short cervix or cervical insufficiency. Ask which structure the finding refers to.

Position during pregnancy and near the due date

A posterior cervix can be a normal finding during pregnancy. As the body prepares for labour the cervix may become softer, shorter, more open and more forward-facing, but these changes do not follow an identical timetable in everyone. It is not required to move forwards at 37 or 38 weeks.

Being posterior after 38 weeks does not prove that labour is far away, that the body has failed to prepare or that a caesarean birth is needed. Position alone cannot reliably predict a delivery date or rule out labour. Your team considers contractions, cervical change over time, gestation and the wellbeing of you and your baby together.

The Bishop score: assessment rather than a countdown

Before induction, a clinician may offer a vaginal examination to assess cervical readiness using a Bishop score. Its components include dilation (opening), effacement or length (thinning or shortening), consistency (firmness or softness), position, and the station of the baby's head in relation to the pelvis. A posterior position generally contributes fewer points than an anterior position, but it is only one component.

The score helps choose an induction method and discuss likely response; it does not provide a precise time of spontaneous labour or guarantee a particular birth outcome. For example, NICE uses a score of 6 or less versus more than 6 to help select cervical-ripening or other induction approaches. Decisions also depend on your history, any previous caesarean, clinical risks and preferences, not a score you calculate at home.

Can the cervix be moved forwards?

There is no routine need to manually reposition a posterior cervix simply to start labour. During a necessary clinical procedure a professional may need to access or gently hold the cervix, but that is different from a treatment that permanently turns it forwards. Do not try to pull, push, stretch or repeatedly examine your own cervix to change its position.

If induction is appropriate, cervical ripening with a medicine or a mechanical method may be discussed, with benefits, risks, monitoring and consent. A membrane sweep is a separate procedure requiring discussion and consent; it is not merely checking position. None of these should be attempted at home or assumed necessary because the cervix is posterior.

How the cervix changes in labour

Cervical ripening includes softening and shortening or thinning; opening is called dilation. These changes may begin before established labour and continue during labour. The cervix often becomes more accessible as labour progresses. Full dilation is approximately 10 cm, allowing the baby to pass through the cervix into the birth canal.

The order and speed of changes vary, and one examination is a snapshot. Progress is assessed alongside contractions, the baby's descent and position, and maternal and fetal wellbeing. A posterior finding alone is neither evidence of obstructed labour nor a reason to ignore symptoms because labour supposedly cannot be starting.

Examinations, discomfort and your consent

A cervix that is harder to reach may make an examination more uncomfortable, but pain is not something you must tolerate. Ask why the examination is needed, what it may change in your care and whether another assessment or a later examination is reasonable. Not every antenatal visit needs a cervical check; vaginal examinations should provide useful clinical information.

The professional should explain the procedure and obtain informed consent, while protecting privacy, dignity and comfort. You may decline before it starts or ask to stop at any point. Discuss a comfortable position, support person or chaperone and pain-relief options where appropriate. Do not perform home checks to confirm labour, particularly if your waters may have broken: contact the maternity team instead.

Outside pregnancy: fertility, screening and IUDs

A posterior cervix can also be a normal anatomical variation outside pregnancy. By itself, it is not a diagnosis of infertility and does not mean sperm cannot reach the uterus. A retroverted uterus is a separate finding and usually does not impair fertility either; associated problems such as endometriosis, pain or scarring may warrant assessment. Seek advice for persistent pelvic pain, painful sex, unusual bleeding or difficulty conceiving rather than attributing everything to position.

Position may make it harder to see the cervix during cervical screening or to access it for an intrauterine device (IUD), but it does not automatically make either impossible. An experienced professional can assess the anatomy and adapt the approach. For screening, changing position or speculum size may help; you can ask to stop. Before IUD placement, uterine position and the cervix are assessed, and an individual pain-management plan should be discussed. Do not skip recommended screening or assume an IUD is unsuitable from the word posterior alone.

When to contact your maternity team

Ask your clinician what was found besides position, why an examination was offered and whether the finding changes the plan. If induction is proposed, ask about the reason, options and your preferences. A posterior cervix is not the same as a short or prematurely opening cervix; those findings require their own history-based assessment and sometimes ultrasound or specialist care.

Contact maternity services immediately if your waters break, you have vaginal bleeding, your baby moves less than usual, or you suspect labour before 37 weeks; do not wait until the next day. Get emergency help for heavy bleeding, severe persistent abdominal pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or if birth seems imminent with a strong urge to push. Follow your own team's labour-contact plan even if a recent examination described a posterior cervix.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NICE guidance supports using cervical readiness to choose induction methods and obtaining consent for vaginal examinations; a position finding is not a delivery timetable.

NHS, RCOG and CDC material informs labour symptoms, distinctions from short cervix, screening adjustments and individual IUD assessment and pain care.

The Victorian government anatomy reference is an older background source, not a new 2026 treatment recommendation; access dates are distinct from publication dates.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the language of an examination and questions to ask. It does not assess your cervix, calculate a Bishop score or decide when labour will start.

When to seek help

Do not attempt to move or repeatedly examine your cervix. Contact maternity services immediately for bleeding, ruptured waters, reduced baby movements or possible labour before 37 weeks. Heavy bleeding, severe persistent pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, or imminent birth need emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Posterior means towards the back of the pelvis; it is a description of cervical position, not a disease by itself.
  • There is no mandatory forwards shift at 37–38 weeks, and position cannot give a reliable labour countdown.
  • The Bishop score supports induction decisions; do not try to calculate it or move the cervix yourself.
  • Examinations need a clinical purpose and consent. New pregnancy warning signs need assessment regardless of the last cervical finding.

Frequently asked questions

Can the cervix be posterior when I am not pregnant?

Yes. It can be a normal anatomical variation. The direction of the cervix should not be confused with the tilt of the whole uterus or a diagnosis such as a short cervix. Symptoms or a separate abnormal finding may still need assessment.

Does a posterior cervix prevent pregnancy?

Position alone is not a diagnosis of infertility and does not mean sperm cannot reach the uterus. If conception is taking longer than expected or you have pain or other symptoms, seek an individual assessment rather than assuming position is the cause.

Will cervical screening or an IUD be impossible?

Not necessarily. Access may be more difficult, but a clinician can assess the anatomy and adjust the approach or arrange further help. Discuss comfort and pain management, and ask to stop if needed. The position label alone is not a reason to miss screening or rule out an IUD.

Is a posterior cervix dangerous in pregnancy?

By itself it is often a normal finding, not evidence of a dangerous pregnancy. It is different from shortening or opening too early. Your symptoms, history and the wellbeing of you and your baby determine whether further assessment is needed.

Must it move forwards by 38 weeks?

No. Cervical changes vary, and there is no required shift at a particular week. A posterior cervix after 38 weeks does not establish that labour is far away or that you need a caesarean.

Can I move it or check dilation at home?

Do not try to reposition, stretch or repeatedly check it. Home examination cannot reliably determine readiness or diagnose labour. Contact the maternity team for symptoms, especially if your waters may have broken.

What does a lower Bishop score mean?

It describes the combined findings of opening, thinning or length, softness, position and the baby's head station. It can guide cervical-ripening and induction choices, but does not predict an exact birth time or guarantee an outcome.

Can I refuse or stop a vaginal examination?

Yes. Ask why it is recommended and how it will affect care. Informed consent, privacy and comfort matter, and you may decline beforehand or ask to stop at any point. The team can discuss alternatives and any implications of delaying the examination.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
